title: Build a Research and Ideation Agent with LangGraph
objective: Frame a production-oriented Python journey around one recurring agent.

title: The finish line
objective: Make the observable outcome, success criteria, and scope explicit.

title: The assistant we will build
objective: Introduce the recurring research-to-decision workflow.
learnerQuestion: What must this assistant actually do?
coreClaim: The assistant is a controlled workflow: decompose, research in parallel, merge evidence, generate and critique ideas, pause for a decision, then finalize.
mechanism: Deterministic graph stages surround model- and tool-driven nodes, with a persisted human gate before finalization.
example: A product lead asks for evidence-backed ideas for reducing onboarding abandonment.
counterpoint: A single model prompt can draft ideas faster, but cannot expose or recover each operational phase independently.
sourceTreatment: Official docs establish mixed deterministic/model orchestration; the anchor architecture is a practitioner design.
visual: Two-row HTML graph showing fan-out, merge, critique loop, and human gate.
practicalTakeaway: Choose graph stages from product and recovery boundaries, not from prompt paragraphs.

title: Use a graph when control is part of the product
objective: Distinguish an open agent loop from explicit orchestration.
learnerQuestion: Why not use one tool-calling loop?
coreClaim: LangGraph earns its complexity when phase order, parallel work, pause/resume, and recovery change correctness or user trust.
mechanism: The graph exposes state and routes as program structure, while a high-level agent loop lets the model decide repeated tool use.
example: Research can fan out, but final publication must wait for evidence merge and human selection.
counterpoint: For a read-only model/tool loop without custom phases, LangChain create_agent is usually the smaller abstraction.
sourceTreatment: Sources establish abstraction levels; the selection rule is an explicitly labeled practitioner inference.
visual: Agent loop and explicit workflow compared side by side.
practicalTakeaway: Do not choose a graph merely because the application uses an LLM.

title: A graph has a static plan and a dynamic run
objective: Build a mental model of topology, state, tasks, and supersteps.
learnerQuestion: What runs when I invoke a compiled graph?
coreClaim: The builder defines possible execution; the runtime schedules eligible node tasks in supersteps and applies their state updates.
mechanism: Edges create tasks, nodes return partial updates, reducers merge writes, and checkpoints capture superstep boundaries.
example: Three research tasks execute in one superstep before synthesis becomes eligible.
counterpoint: A diagram shows possible routes, not the exact route or data of a particular run.
sourceTreatment: Official Graph API and persistence docs define runtime and superstep behavior.
visual: Definition lane above a run lane with evolving state snapshots.
practicalTakeaway: Debug the executed state transition, not only the drawn graph.

title: State is the workflow contract
objective: Teach state as durable data and interface, not a scratch dictionary.
learnerQuestion: What belongs in graph state?
coreClaim: State should hold durable facts needed by later nodes, routing, recovery, or inspection; dependencies and large authoritative datasets belong elsewhere.
mechanism: Typed state keys define node interfaces and checkpoint payloads, while runtime context injects dependencies and stores retain cross-thread data.
example: Keep the brief, research topics, normalized findings, ideas, and review decision; inject a search client and keep source documents in their source system.
counterpoint: Persisting more data can simplify a prototype but increases checkpoint size, privacy exposure, and migration burden.
sourceTreatment: Sources define state/checkpointer/store boundaries; inclusion criteria are practitioner guidance.
visual: State / runtime context / store / source-system boundary map.
practicalTakeaway: For each key, name its owner, lifetime, reducer, and retention policy.

title: Reducers are concurrency policy
objective: Explain how multiple node writes become one state value.
learnerQuestion: What happens when parallel nodes update the same key?
coreClaim: Without an explicit reducer, a state key overwrites; parallel writes to one key require a merge rule such as list concatenation.
mechanism: An Annotated state field attaches a reducer that folds node updates into the channel value.
example: Three research tasks each return one finding list and operator.add merges them into the parent findings list.
counterpoint: List concatenation does not provide deterministic completion order or deduplication.
sourceTreatment: Official guide defines reducers and warns that parallel update order is not stable.
visual: Parallel writes compared with and without an operator.add reducer.
practicalTakeaway: Treat every reducer as application logic and test identity, associativity, ordering, and duplicates.

title: Practice — repair the state contract
objective: Make the learner diagnose a concurrent update instead of memorizing reducer syntax.
prompt: Three research tasks return findings to one list key with no reducer. Predict the failure or overwrite behavior, then specify a safe state definition and deterministic ordering strategy.
expectedReasoning: Add an Annotated list reducer such as operator.add; attach a stable topic or rank to every finding; sort after the barrier because parallel completion order is not guaranteed.
visual: Broken state declaration, three task outputs, and revealed repair.

title: A node boundary is a recovery boundary
objective: Choose node granularity using operational criteria.
learnerQuestion: How large should a node be?
coreClaim: Separate work when it needs an independent retry policy, checkpoint, trace, approval, or failure owner; keep pure helpers inside a node.
mechanism: A failed or interrupted node restarts from its beginning, while completed prior nodes remain checkpointed.
example: Research API calls, synthesis, human review, and final publication are distinct nodes; text cleanup is a helper.
counterpoint: Too many tiny nodes create topology noise, state plumbing, and trace overhead.
sourceTreatment: Official guidance ties node granularity to retry, checkpoint, and observability boundaries.
visual: One large node split only at meaningful failure boundaries.
practicalTakeaway: Draw a node around a unit you are willing to rerun as one operation.

title: Four control primitives, four different jobs
objective: Differentiate static edges, conditional edges, Send, and Command.
learnerQuestion: Which routing primitive should I use?
coreClaim: Use static edges for invariant order, conditional edges for external routing functions, Send for dynamic fan-out, and Command when a node must update state and choose its next hop together.
mechanism: Each primitive creates different task scheduling and graph-visualization semantics.
example: Plan always precedes research; plan emits one Send per topic; review returns a Command to revise or finalize.
counterpoint: Command can hide topology inside node code, so conditional edges may be easier to inspect when state updates and routing are separable.
sourceTreatment: Official examples define each primitive; the selection table is synthesis.
visual: Four miniature topologies with trigger, return value, and best-fit condition.
practicalTakeaway: Pick the primitive that makes the routing decision visible at its natural boundary.

title: Practice — predict the accidental double route
objective: Reveal how static and dynamic routing can combine unexpectedly.
prompt: A review node has a normal edge to finalize and also returns Command(goto='revise') when rejected. Which nodes become eligible, and how would you repair the graph?
expectedReasoning: The normal edge still schedules finalize while Command schedules revise. Remove the normal outgoing edge and let Command own both destinations, or move routing into one conditional edge.
visual: Broken topology with two highlighted outgoing paths and a corrected topology.

title: Send turns a plan into a dynamic parallel superstep
objective: Trace map-reduce scheduling and its barrier.
learnerQuestion: How does research fan-out and join?
coreClaim: A conditional route can return one Send per topic; those research tasks run in the same superstep, their reducer-backed writes merge, and synthesis waits for the superstep to finish.
mechanism: Send supplies task-specific input while downstream edge scheduling forms a barrier before the shared successor.
example: Market, user, and risk research complete in arbitrary order before one synthesis call sees all findings.
counterpoint: Parallelism reduces wall time only when external limits, model quotas, and downstream bottlenecks permit it.
sourceTreatment: Official Send and superstep docs support the scheduling semantics.
visual: Timeline with one plan task, three research tasks, reducer merge, and one synthesis task.
practicalTakeaway: Make merge semantics and concurrency limits part of the design, not afterthoughts.

title: Define state for the run you need to recover
objective: Show the verified Python state and reducer contract.
learnerQuestion: What does the anchor state look like in Python?
coreClaim: A small typed state with normalized findings and an explicit reducer is enough to support fan-out, review, and recovery.
mechanism: TypedDict fields document the contract; Annotated findings use operator.add for task aggregation.
example: The runnable example defines ResearchState and a smaller ResearchTask payload for Send.

exampleValidation.expected: Two tests pass, including parallel findings aggregation and interrupt/resume.

counterpoint: TypedDict validates static shape, not runtime values from a model or external API.
sourceTreatment: Code follows the official Graph API and is verified against the pinned release.
visual: Focused code excerpt with state-key responsibilities annotated.
practicalTakeaway: Normalize external outputs before writing them into durable state.

title: Compile the smallest useful topology
objective: Show verified graph construction without model-provider noise.
learnerQuestion: How do the nodes and routes connect?
coreClaim: The anchor graph needs one dynamic fan-out, a reducer-backed join, an interrupting review node, and Command-based review routing.
mechanism: StateGraph registers nodes and edges, then compiles with a checkpointer for durable review.
example: START → plan → Send(research...) → synthesize → review → finalize → END.

exampleValidation.expected: The graph pauses at review and reaches finalize only after an approve resume command.

counterpoint: Search and model adapters are deterministic stand-ins in this example so orchestration can be tested without credentials.
sourceTreatment: Verified code uses documented primitives; the slide labels its stand-ins.
visual: Code excerpt paired with the resulting graph topology.
practicalTakeaway: Prove control flow with fakes before adding nondeterministic providers.

title: Practice — trace one run
objective: Make the learner connect topology, state updates, supersteps, and checkpoints.
prompt: For the onboarding brief, predict the next eligible node(s), changed state keys, and checkpoint boundary after plan, parallel research, synthesis, interrupt, and resume.
expectedReasoning: Plan writes topics; Send schedules three research tasks; their findings merge at one superstep; synthesis writes ideas; review pauses and checkpoints; resume restarts review and Command routes to finalize.
visual: Trace table with fragment-revealed answers.

title: Keep evidence facts separate from generated prose
objective: Design model and tool adapters around normalized evidence.
learnerQuestion: Where do search, LLMs, and citations belong?
coreClaim: Research nodes should emit structured evidence records; synthesis should consume those records and produce ideas with evidence references rather than hiding sources inside prompt text.
mechanism: Adapters validate tool output into source URL, claim, excerpt or locator, retrieval time, and provenance before state update.
example: An idea cites finding IDs market-2 and user-1, allowing a later verifier to inspect support.
counterpoint: A URL in state is provenance, not proof that the source supports the claim.
sourceTreatment: Official docs support raw state and evaluation decomposition; evidence schema is practitioner guidance.
visual: Tool output → normalized finding → idea citation data flow.
practicalTakeaway: Design an evidence contract before designing the synthesis prompt.

title: Loops need budgets and an observable exit
objective: Make critique/refinement loops bounded and diagnosable.
learnerQuestion: How should the agent decide to revise or stop?
coreClaim: A critique loop needs explicit quality signals, a revision budget, and a terminal fallback; model self-confidence alone is not a stopping rule.
mechanism: The critic writes structured gaps and scores; a route checks thresholds and attempt count before revising, interrupting, or continuing.
example: Revise once if evidence coverage is below 80%; then route to human review with the unresolved gaps.
counterpoint: More refinement calls can amplify the same blind spot and consume budget without improving evidence.
sourceTreatment: Loop APIs and evaluation lifecycle are sourced; thresholds are illustrative product policy.
visual: Bounded critique loop with quality gate and max-attempt escape.
practicalTakeaway: Every cycle needs a counter, exit condition, and failure artifact.

title: Resume restarts the interrupted node
objective: Teach the exact interrupt re-execution hazard.
learnerQuestion: Where does execution resume after human input?
coreClaim: LangGraph restores state but restarts the entire node containing interrupt; code before the interrupt runs again.
mechanism: interrupt signals the runtime to checkpoint and pause; Command(resume=...) supplies the saved interrupt's return value on node re-execution.
example: The review node may render a proposal before interrupt, but final publication must happen in a later node.
counterpoint: An interrupt feels like a suspended Python call, but its operational semantics are replay from the node boundary.
sourceTreatment: Directly supported by official interrupt rules.
visual: First-run and resumed-run timeline with the review node shown twice.
practicalTakeaway: Put interrupt first, or keep all pre-interrupt work idempotent.

title: Pause and resume on the same thread
objective: Show verified interrupt invocation and resume code.
learnerQuestion: What does the application call?
coreClaim: A durable human review requires a checkpointer, a stable thread_id, an interrupt payload, and a later Command(resume=...) using the same thread configuration.
mechanism: The first invoke returns an interrupt marker; the application stores the thread identity and resumes after authorization and validation.
example: The test reads paused ideas from graph.get_state(config), selects one, then resumes with an approve decision.

exampleValidation.expected: The paused snapshot points to review; the resumed result contains a final_brief and approval.

counterpoint: Thread IDs are access-control-sensitive identifiers and must not be accepted without authorization.
sourceTreatment: Verified example follows official resume flow; authorization warning is application guidance.
visual: Two short code blocks connected by a persisted thread identity.
practicalTakeaway: Treat resume as an authenticated state-changing API call.

title: Four data scopes, four different owners
objective: Separate graph state, checkpoint history, long-term store, and source truth.
learnerQuestion: Where should each kind of data live?
coreClaim: Run state, checkpoint history, cross-thread memory, and authoritative evidence have different lifetimes and access patterns.
mechanism: State is the current contract; checkpointers persist thread snapshots; stores persist application-defined cross-thread items; external systems own source documents and business truth.
example: Selected idea is thread state, user preferences are store data, source pages remain in the research corpus, and publication status lives in the product database.
counterpoint: One physical Postgres cluster can host several scopes, but logical ownership and retention must remain distinct.
sourceTreatment: Official docs define checkpointer/store scope; source-system boundary is practitioner architecture.
visual: Nested scope map with lifetimes and owners.
practicalTakeaway: Do not turn checkpoint history into an accidental system of record.

title: Checkpoint boundaries define the recovery unit
objective: Explain checkpoints, pending writes, and parallel failure recovery.
learnerQuestion: What repeats after a failure?
coreClaim: Full checkpoints occur at superstep boundaries, while pending task writes let completed parallel siblings survive a failure within the same superstep.
mechanism: On resume, LangGraph can reuse successful task writes and rerun failed work from the prior safe boundary.
example: If risk research fails after market and user research finish, the successful findings need not be recomputed.
counterpoint: External API side effects are not made idempotent simply because their returned state write is durable.
sourceTreatment: Official persistence docs describe checkpoints and pending writes.
visual: Parallel superstep with two durable task writes and one failed task.
practicalTakeaway: Align expensive calls with node boundaries and give side effects idempotency keys.

title: Replay reproduces a path; fork explores another
objective: Use checkpoint history for debugging and alternative decisions.
learnerQuestion: How can I revisit an earlier run?
coreClaim: Replay resumes from a prior checkpoint; fork updates state at a checkpoint and creates an alternative trajectory, with all downstream model and API work running again.
mechanism: Checkpoint IDs address historical state; update_state creates a new checkpoint rather than rewriting history.
example: Fork before synthesis with a narrower audience and compare the new ideas to the original run.
counterpoint: A fork is not bit-for-bit reproduction when downstream calls are nondeterministic or external data changed.
sourceTreatment: Official time-travel guide defines replay and fork semantics.
visual: Checkpoint timeline that branches before synthesis.
practicalTakeaway: Record model, prompt, tool, and data versions when comparison matters.

title: Memory is not the same as research evidence
objective: Separate thread continuity, preferences, and cited evidence.
learnerQuestion: What should the assistant remember?
coreClaim: Use checkpointed state for thread continuity and a store for durable preferences; keep evidence as explicit sourced records with freshness and provenance.
mechanism: Short-term memory is thread-scoped state, while long-term memory uses namespaced store items across threads.
example: Remember the user's preferred tone across projects, but re-research a time-sensitive market claim.
counterpoint: Semantic retrieval from memory can surface stale or incorrectly generalized facts.
sourceTreatment: Official docs define memory scopes; evidence freshness guidance is practitioner inference.
visual: Thread state, preference store, and evidence corpus compared by lifetime and trust.
practicalTakeaway: Give every remembered item a scope, provenance, and expiry rule.

title: A subgraph is a state-lifetime boundary
objective: Choose per-invocation, per-thread, or stateless subgraphs deliberately.
learnerQuestion: When should research become a subgraph?
coreClaim: Use subgraphs for independently testable capabilities or distinct state lifetimes, not as decorative agent roles.
mechanism: Default per-invocation subgraphs inherit parent persistence for one call; checkpointer=True keeps per-thread state; checkpointer=False removes durability.
example: A one-off source-analysis worker should usually be per-invocation, while a multi-turn research coach may need per-thread memory.
counterpoint: Per-thread subgraphs can conflict when the same instance is invoked concurrently and add checkpoint complexity.
sourceTreatment: Official guide defines persistence modes and their concurrency limits.
visual: Three-column subgraph persistence comparison.
practicalTakeaway: Choose subgraph persistence from state lifetime and concurrency, not from the word 'agent'.

title: Prefer capability boundaries over agent theater
objective: Apply subgraphs to a pragmatic research architecture.
learnerQuestion: Should every research role be its own agent?
coreClaim: Split a capability only when it needs its own tools, state, policy, tests, or owner; parallel node tasks are sufficient for homogeneous research topics.
mechanism: Send handles scaled copies of one worker; subgraphs encapsulate a richer multi-step capability with an explicit interface.
example: Use Send for market/user/risk topics; use a subgraph for source verification if it has retrieval, contradiction checks, and its own quality policy.
counterpoint: Multiple persona prompts can increase cost and coordination failure without adding a real boundary.
sourceTreatment: Mechanisms are sourced; capability-versus-persona guidance is practitioner inference.
visual: Send workers versus a stateful verification subgraph.
practicalTakeaway: Name components after accountable capabilities, not fictional job titles.

title: Stream progress, tokens, and diagnostics separately
objective: Design a useful run protocol for the product UI.
learnerQuestion: What should the user see while the graph runs?
coreClaim: State updates, model tokens, custom progress, and debug events are different streams with different consumers and privacy requirements.
mechanism: stream and astream accept modes such as updates, messages, custom, checkpoints, tasks, and debug; v2 returns a unified StreamPart shape.
example: Show '3/5 sources checked' from custom events while streaming final prose tokens from messages and retaining task events for operators.
counterpoint: Debug streams can expose prompts, sources, or sensitive state and should not be sent directly to end users.
sourceTreatment: Official streaming docs define modes and versioned formats.
visual: One graph event lane multiplexed into user, developer, and operator consumers.
practicalTakeaway: Define a stable application event schema over framework stream events.

title: Classify failures by who can resolve them
objective: Turn errors into explicit recovery paths.
learnerQuestion: Should this failure retry, loop, interrupt, or crash?
coreClaim: Transient infrastructure failures retry; model-correctable failures loop with structured feedback; user-correctable failures interrupt; programming and invariant failures surface.
mechanism: Per-node RetryPolicy, graph routes, interrupt, and exception propagation express different ownership.
example: HTTP 503 retries, missing evidence loops to research, ambiguous scope asks the user, and an impossible state assertion aborts.
counterpoint: Catching every exception and asking the model to recover hides defects and can create costly loops.
sourceTreatment: Official docs provide the error taxonomy and retry behavior.
visual: Failure-owner taxonomy leading to four mechanisms.
practicalTakeaway: Write the recovery owner beside each node's expected failures.

title: Practice — choose the recovery mechanism
objective: Apply the failure taxonomy to realistic research failures.
prompt: Route four cases: search returns 503; synthesis produces an unsupported claim; the brief omits target users; normalized state violates its schema. Choose retry, loop, interrupt, or surface and explain why.
expectedReasoning: 503 is transient and retryable; unsupported claim is model/workflow-correctable and loops with evidence gaps; missing users needs human input and interrupts; schema violation is a defect/invariant failure and surfaces. Alpha node timeout/error-handler APIs should not be assumed stable.
visual: Decision matrix with fragment-revealed placements.

title: Test topology and nodes before testing prose
objective: Build a deterministic graph test strategy.
learnerQuestion: What can I assert exactly?
coreClaim: Unit tests should prove state updates, routing, reducer behavior, interrupt points, and resume transitions with fakes before any model-quality evaluation.
mechanism: Create a fresh graph/checkpointer per test, invoke individual compiled nodes when useful, and seed checkpoint state for partial execution.
example: The bundled unittest proves three findings merge and finalization cannot occur before approval.
counterpoint: Passing deterministic tests says nothing about live search quality, citation support, or idea usefulness.
sourceTreatment: Official testing guide supports node and partial graph testing; bundled tests are verified examples.
visual: Test layers from reducer/unit to partial path to end-to-end run.
practicalTakeaway: Separate orchestration correctness from model quality so failures are diagnosable.

title: Evaluate the evidence path, not only the final answer
objective: Define quality measures for a research and ideation system.
learnerQuestion: What does good mean for this agent?
coreClaim: Research quality requires component and trajectory measures—source coverage, support, diversity, contradiction handling, idea distinctness, and human acceptance—not one final-text score.
mechanism: Offline datasets compare versions before release; sampled online evaluations and human feedback turn production failures into new regression cases.
example: A run can score high on writing quality yet fail because two of five claims lack supporting evidence.
counterpoint: LLM judges are useful signals but need calibration, deterministic checks, and human review for consequential claims.
sourceTreatment: Official evaluation docs define offline/online and graph evaluation; metrics are tailored practitioner guidance.
visual: Layered evaluation stack with component, trajectory, outcome, and production feedback measures.
practicalTakeaway: Attach at least one metric to each critical node and one to the end-user outcome.

title: Trace decisions with versions and cost context
objective: Make graph behavior observable and comparable across releases.
learnerQuestion: What should a production trace record?
coreClaim: A useful trace links thread, run, node, model, tool, prompt, source, latency, token cost, retries, and human feedback without leaking sensitive content.
mechanism: LangSmith structures projects, traces, runs, and threads and accepts tags and metadata; equivalent telemetry can use other systems.
example: Filter unsupported-claim failures by graph version and research provider, then add representative traces to an offline dataset.
counterpoint: Full payload logging can violate privacy or data-residency rules and increase cost.
sourceTreatment: Official observability model supports trace structure; minimum metadata set is practitioner guidance.
visual: Trace tree annotated with version, latency, cost, and feedback fields.
practicalTakeaway: Log enough to reproduce a decision, and redact enough to preserve trust.

title: Production is a topology, not a compile call
objective: Place the graph in a deployable system architecture.
learnerQuestion: What surrounds the graph in production?
coreClaim: The graph runtime depends on authenticated APIs, durable persistence, stores, source systems, tool services, review UI, telemetry, and background execution.
mechanism: A compiled graph is exposed by Agent Server or a self-hosted service; external components retain their own ownership and guarantees.
example: The review UI resumes an authorized thread; research tools fetch sources; a durable checkpointer restores execution; traces feed evaluation.
counterpoint: Managed LangSmith deployment can supply much of this runtime infrastructure, but it is one hosting choice rather than a LangGraph requirement.
sourceTreatment: Official docs support deployment and persistence options; architecture combines them into one system view.
visual: HTML production topology with trust, state, and telemetry boundaries.
practicalTakeaway: Review every arrow for authentication, timeout, retry, idempotency, and data retention.

title: Harden the graph before adding autonomy
objective: Translate production depth into an actionable readiness checklist.
learnerQuestion: What must be true before real users rely on it?
coreClaim: Production readiness requires bounded work, least-privilege tools, durable state, idempotent effects, schema validation, privacy controls, quality gates, and operational rollback.
mechanism: Budgets and recursion limits constrain execution; tool services enforce authorization; deployment config pins dependencies; checkpoints and version metadata support controlled recovery.
example: Cap sources and revisions, validate every finding, redact sensitive source text, require approval for publication, and canary a new graph version.
counterpoint: No checklist removes the need for incident response and domain-specific risk analysis.
sourceTreatment: Framework controls are sourced; security and release checklist is practitioner synthesis.
visual: Preflight checklist organized by execution, data, tools, quality, and operations.
practicalTakeaway: Increase autonomy only after the corresponding recovery and evidence mechanisms exist.

title: What LangGraph buys you
objective: Summarize benefits as mechanisms rather than marketing labels.
learnerQuestion: What concrete advantage does the graph provide?
coreClaim: LangGraph provides explicit mixed control, durable pause/resume, checkpointed recovery, parallel scheduling, state inspection, and testable boundaries.
mechanism: StateGraph primitives and the Pregel-style runtime turn these requirements into reusable execution semantics.
example: The research assistant can resume after review, reuse completed parallel work, and expose a trace of how evidence became an idea.
counterpoint: These are orchestration capabilities; they do not make models accurate, tools safe, or prompts good.
sourceTreatment: Benefits map directly to documented mechanisms.
visual: Benefit-to-mechanism mapping, avoiding generic feature cards.
practicalTakeaway: Adopt LangGraph for the runtime property you can name and test.

title: The costs are real—choose the smallest sufficient runtime
objective: Compare plain Python, create_agent, and LangGraph with exit criteria.
learnerQuestion: When is LangGraph the wrong choice?
coreClaim: LangGraph adds state-schema, routing, persistence, migration, concurrency, and observability design work; simpler runtimes are preferable when those controls do not change the outcome.
mechanism: Framework choice follows required control: linear deterministic work fits plain Python, standard model/tool loops fit create_agent, and custom durable workflows fit LangGraph.
example: A one-shot brainstorm stays a function; a search chatbot uses create_agent; an approval-gated research pipeline uses LangGraph.
counterpoint: Starting high-level does not prevent dropping to LangGraph later because LangChain agents already run on its runtime.
sourceTreatment: Sources establish abstraction relationships; cost and selection criteria are labeled practitioner inference.
visual: Three-column decision table with fit, warning sign, and upgrade trigger.
practicalTakeaway: Choose the lowest abstraction level whose guarantees match the product.
